title: Hinduism: the act, not the fruit
hook: Krishna tells Arjuna to act without clinging to results (Bhagavad Gita 2.47)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the father, the son and the salt: tat tvam asi. Your line was you are that. Did salt in your food remind you of the cup of water? Day two hundred thirty-five.

You send the job application, and then you check your email forty times. You post the thing, and then you watch the likes. You cook for someone, and then you study their face on the first bite. The work was done an hour ago, but your mind is still stuck on what comes back. The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, has a line about exactly this, spoken on a battlefield, to a man so frozen by consequences he can't lift his bow. Today's word: karma yoga.
screen: `CHECKING YOUR EMAIL FORTY TIMES.` → `A MAN WHO CAN'T LIFT HIS BOW.` → `KARMA YOGA.`

segments.voice: The Gita is set at the edge of a great battle in the epic Mahabharata. The warrior Arjuna looks across the field and sees his own cousins, teachers and elders on the other side. He drops his bow and says he won't fight. His charioteer is Krishna, whom Hindus revere as God come to earth. What follows is their conversation, and it makes up the whole Gita. In chapter two, verse forty-seven, Krishna says, roughly: you have a right to your action, but never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting, and don't let that turn you toward doing nothing, either. That's karma yoga. Karma here means action, simply what you do. Yoga is traced to a root meaning to yoke, to join: a discipline, a path. So karma yoga is the path of action, of doing your work fully while letting go of your grip on how it turns out. Notice what Krishna doesn't say. He doesn't say results don't matter, or that you shouldn't care. He says the doing is yours; the outcome isn't in your hands, so don't chain yourself to it. Later in the Gita, Krishna adds that whatever a person does can be offered to him, as worship. Hindus have read this battlefield in more than one way. Some take it as a real war and a warrior's real duty. Others, Mahatma Gandhi among them, read the battle as the struggle inside every person. Either way, the line fits a weekday at a desk. Do the task. Do it well. Then open your hand.
screen: `ARJUNA DROPS HIS BOW.` · `A RIGHT TO THE ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.` · `KARMA, ACTION; YOGA, A PATH.` · `DO IT FULLY, THEN OPEN YOUR HAND.` · then, large: `THE ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one task to do, dropping the outcome. Settle and breathe. Pick one thing you'll do after this: an email, a meal, a conversation. Picture yourself doing it fully, with care, as well as you can. Now picture the moment it's done, and imagine opening your hand, palm up, and letting the result go wherever it goes. Try opening your actual hand now. The bell holds the time.
Karma yoga. The path of action: do your work fully, and let go of clinging to its fruits, as Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita. Today's word.
Your line: the act, not the fruit. Today, after you finish the task you chose, don't check on it for an hour. Let the doing be enough. Day two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Hindus who follow karma yoga treat it as a way of daily life: doing one's work and duties carefully, often offering them to God, without clinging to the results.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. your own family stands across the field. you've dropped your bow. what does Krishna tell you?
options: go home; nothing is worth this.
act, and let go of clinging to the fruits.
fight only if you're sure to win.
fork.reveal: Krishna tells him he has a right to the action, never to its fruits, and not to turn toward doing nothing either. that's karma yoga.

original.note: Sanskrit: the path, or discipline, of action.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is what comes back to you.
what it means: karma yoga is doing your work fully while letting go of clinging to results.
what a scholar hears: Gita 2.47; karma is from kṛ, to do, yoga from yuj, to yoke; the Gita also teaches paths of knowledge and devotion.
